topic: STEMI Definition and ECG Criteria
content: STEMI = ST-elevation myocardial infarction. ECG diagnostic criteria: ≥1mm ST elevation in contiguous leads (≥2mm in precordial leads V1-V3 acceptable). New LBBB with appropriate concordance also counts as STEMI equivalent. Troponin elevation confirms myocardial necrosis. Requires reperfusion therapy (PCI or fibrinolysis) within 120 minutes to salvage myocardium. Window critical: every minute of delay increases mortality.

topic: NSTEMI and Unstable Angina - Distinction
content: NSTEMI = no ST elevation but troponin elevated (high-sensitivity troponin within hours; conventional troponin 3-6 hours). Unstable angina = chest pain/ACS symptoms but normal troponin (negative predictive value >99% with high-sensitivity troponin at 0 and 2 hours). Both have similar pathophysiology (plaque rupture, partial thrombosis) but better prognosis than STEMI. Risk stratification (TIMI, GRACE) guides medical therapy, catheterization timing, antiplatelet intensity.

topic: Troponin Kinetics and Interpretation
content: Conventional troponin: rises 3-6 hours post-MI, peaks 24-48 hours, normalizes 7-14 days. High-sensitivity troponin: rises within 1-3 hours, higher sensitivity (>99%). Serial troponins improve diagnostic accuracy. Serial change more valuable than single value: delta rise/fall algorithm (>20% relative change suggests acute MI). Elevated troponin not pathognomonic: occurs in sepsis, PE, heart failure, kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, endocarditis. Integration with clinical/ECG findings critical.

topic: ACS Atypical Presentations
content: Atypical ACS presentations increase with: female sex, age >75, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure. Presentations: dyspnea without chest pain (silent MI in elderly/diabetics), epigastric discomfort (confused with GERD), jaw/arm/back pain, syncope, altered mental status, acute decompensated heart failure. Women often have chest discomfort more atypical (nausea, fatigue, shortness of breath). Diabetics have high prevalence of silent MI (autonomic neuropathy). High suspicion needed; obtain ECG/troponin liberally.

topic: Differential Diagnosis of Chest Pain - ACS vs Non-ACS
content: ACS differentials: aortic dissection (sudden, tearing, hypotension, pulse differentials), PE (pleuritic, tachycardia, risk factors), pneumonia (fever, infiltrate, productive cough), pericarditis (pleuritic, positional, pericardial rub, PR depression), GERD (relation to meals, relief with antacids), musculoskeletal pain (reproducible, positional), anxiety (normal ECG/troponin). ECG + troponin + chest X-ray narrow differential. Troponin negative + normal ECG = low risk for ACS (negative predictive value >99%).

topic: TIMI Score for NSTEMI/Unstable Angina
content: TIMI Risk Score (0-7 points): age ≥65 (1), ≥3 CAD risk factors (1), prior CAD (1), aspirin use in past 7 days (1), severe angina ≥2 episodes in 24h (1), ST changes (1), elevated troponin (1). Score 0-1: low risk, 2: intermediate, 3-4: high, 5-7: very high risk. Predicts 14-day mortality/MI/revascularization. Guides antiplatelet intensity (P2Y12 inhibitor dose), timing of catheterization (within 24h for high risk, can delay low risk).

topic: GRACE Score for Risk Prediction
content: GRACE Score (Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events): incorporates age, HR, SBP, creatinine, Killip class, ST deviation, troponin elevation, in-hospital mortality/6-month mortality. More comprehensive than TIMI. Score <100: low risk. 100-140: intermediate. >140: high risk. Predicts longer-term outcomes. Used to risk-stratify for invasive vs conservative strategy. Online calculator available. Particularly useful when multiple risk factors present or uncertainty about stratification.

topic: ACS - Acute Presentation and Initial Stabilization
content: ACS patient initial management: oxygen if SpO2 <90%, IV access (large bore), continuous cardiac monitoring, ECG within 10 minutes, troponin/CBC/CMP/coagulation studies, chest X-ray, pain control (morphine 2-4mg IV, repeat q5-15min), urgent cardiology consultation. Nitrates if hypertensive/pulmonary edema (caution if RV infarction). Beta-blocker if tachycardia/hypertension (avoid if AV block/shock). ACE inhibitor early if tolerating. Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) immediately for all ACS.

topic: ECG Localization - LAD Territory Infarction
content: Left anterior descending (LAD) STEMI: ST elevation in V1-V4, I, aVL. Extensive anterior MI if involves V1-V4, I, aVL (high mortality). Diagonal branch involvement: ST elevation V1-V4, aVL, but not II, III, aVF. Associated: high-degree AV block (LAD septal perforator), Mobitz II, complete heart block, anterior wall rupture (mechanical complications), cardiogenic shock common. Loss of septal Q waves suggests septal necrosis.

topic: ECG Localization - RCA Territory Infarction
content: Right coronary artery (RCA) STEMI: ST elevation II, III, aVF (inferior wall). Right ventricular involvement: ST elevation V4R (right-sided ECG lead). Associated: bradycardia (sinus node involvement), high-degree AV block (proximal RCA at nodal artery), hypotension (RV infarction), usually better prognosis than LAD. KEY: RV infarction contraindication = nitrates/IV morphine (preload-dependent; use caution). Fluid bolus may help restore blood pressure.

topic: ECG Localization - Left Circumflex Territory and Posterior MI
content: Left circumflex (LCx) STEMI: ST elevation I, aVL, sometimes V5-V6. Posterior wall MI: ST depression V1-V3 (reciprocal changes) with ST elevation in posterior leads (V7-V9 on right side, or use posterior precordial leads). Posterior MI can be subtle; evaluate posterior leads if inferior/posterior symptoms. LCx occlusion at distal margin: mild involvement; proximal: extends to RV. Prognosis intermediate between LAD and RCA.

topic: Right Ventricular Infarction - Recognition and Management
content: RV infarction: occurs in ~50% of inferior wall MIs. ST elevation V4R (right-sided ECG) diagnostic. Presentation: hypotension disproportionate to MI size, elevated JVP, clear lung fields (unlike LV failure). Management: fluid bolus (crystalloid) cautiously to restore RV filling (critical for RV output). AVOID nitrates and morphine (decrease preload, worsen shock). AVOID beta-blockers if bradycardic (AV block already present). Maintain HR 60-80 and BP >90. RV infarction usually recovers within days.

topic: STEMI Reperfusion - PCI vs Fibrinolysis
content: Primary PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention) preferred over fibrinolysis if available within 120 minutes door-to-balloon time. PCI advantages: higher TIMI 3 flow, lower reocclusion, better mortality (7-8% vs 9-10% for fibrinolysis). Fibrinolysis: faster door-to-needle (30 min), useful if PCI delay >120 min, patient transfer >90 min, or PCI unavailable. Contraindications to fibrinolysis: active bleeding, prior ICH, recent surgery, aortic dissection. Early transfer for PCI reasonable if <3 hours from symptom onset even if fibrinolysis initiated.

topic: Aspirin in ACS - Dosing and Mechanism
content: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid): irreversible COX inhibition, platelet aggregation inhibition. Loading dose: 325-500mg PO (chewed for faster absorption) or 250-500mg IV. Maintenance: 81-325mg daily (higher doses increase GI bleed risk). Onset: 15-30 minutes. Side effects: GI bleed (especially with concurrent NSAID/corticosteroids), bleeding complications, drug allergy (rash, anaphylaxis). Hold for ≥5 days before elective surgery if possible (platelet dysfunction persists). Use in all ACS unless contraindicated (allergy, active bleeding).

topic: P2Y12 Inhibitors - Clopidogrel, Ticagrelor, Prasugrel
content: Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) = aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor. Clopidogrel (Plavix): 600mg loading (or 300mg), 75mg daily. Slower onset, prodrug requiring CYP3A4 metabolism. Ticagrelor (Brilinta): 180mg loading, 60mg BID. Faster onset, stronger P2Y12 binding, reversible. Prasugrel (Effient): 60mg loading (5mg if <60kg/age >75), 5mg daily. Fastest onset, strongest platelet inhibition, higher bleeding risk. Ticagrelor preferred over clopidogrel in STEMI (faster). Prasugrel reserved for angiography-proven CAD. All require DDP-DES or BMS placement for DAPT duration.

topic: DAPT Duration - Balancing Stent Thrombosis vs Bleeding
content: DAPT duration: typically 12 months for ACS (STEMI or NSTEMI). Bare-metal stents (BMS): minimum 1 month, then aspirin monotherapy. Drug-eluting stents (DES): minimum 3-6 months, typically extend to 12 months for ACS. Shorter duration (3-6 months): consider if high bleeding risk (age, renal disease, anemia, oral anticoagulant needed). Longer duration (>12 months): consider if low bleeding risk, high thrombotic risk (diabetes, complex anatomy, prior stent thrombosis). Aspirin monotherapy indefinitely post-DAPT.

topic: Beta-Blockers in ACS - Acute and Long-term Use
content: Beta-blockers reduce mortality post-MI (15-20% relative risk reduction). Acute use: reduce cardiac work, heart rate, blood pressure. IV metoprolol 25-50mg, then PO maintenance (target HR 50-60). Esmolol for temporary control. Cautions: avoid if bradycardia <50, hypotension, AV block, decompensated heart failure, RV infarction (loss of RV chronotropic support). Continue long-term post-MI unless contraindicated. Cardioselective agents (metoprolol, atenolol) preferred over non-selective (propranolol).

topic: ACE Inhibitors in ACS - Indication and Timing
content: ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril): reduce LV remodeling post-MI, lower mortality 20%, particularly if anterior MI or reduced EF (<40%). Start within 24-48 hours (after acute stabilization, BP adequate). Dose: lisinopril 5mg daily, titrate to 10-40mg daily. Cautions: hyperkalemia risk (especially if renal disease), hypotension, cough (15-20%). Check renal function, potassium before/after initiation. Continue indefinitely unless contraindicated. ARBs (losartan) alternative if ACE-I intolerant (cough).

topic: Statins in ACS - High-Intensity Therapy
content: High-intensity statins reduce LDL, reduce cardiovascular events/mortality. Acute MI: initiate high-dose statin immediately (atorvastatin 80mg daily or rosuvastatin 40mg daily) regardless of baseline LDL. Continue indefinitely. LDL target: <70 mg/dL (or <55 if very high risk). Side effects: myalgia (rare but significant statin intolerance), elevated transaminases (monitor baseline), myositis/rhabdomyolysis (rare), drug interactions (avoid certain statins with CYP3A4 inhibitors). Check lipid panel, CK baseline. Benefits far outweigh risks in ACS.

topic: Nitroglycerin in ACS - Uses and Precautions
content: Nitrates: reduce preload, afterload, coronary vasodilation (improves collateral blood flow). Acute use: SL nitroglycerin 0.3-0.6mg q5 minutes x 3 doses (within 10 minutes of symptom onset). IV nitroglycerin for ongoing chest pain or hypertension/pulmonary edema. Cautions: avoid if hypotensive (SBP <90), RV infarction (preload-dependent), concurrent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil = profound hypotension). Tolerance develops with continuous use; use dosing intervals to prevent. Long-term nitrate use limited in ACS (no mortality benefit).

topic: Morphine in ACS - Analgesia and Hemodynamic Effects
content: Morphine: potent opioid analgesia, anxiolysis, reduces preload (mild), decreases adrenergic tone. Dosing: 2-4mg IV, repeat q5-15 min until pain controlled. Side effects: respiratory depression, hypotension, bradycardia (via vagal effect), histamine release (caution in aspiration risk). Caution: avoid in inferior MI with RV involvement (preload-dependent) or cardiogenic shock. Modern trend: less reliance on morphine (increases heart rate via compensation, may worsen ischemia); use cautiously, preferring beta-blockers/nitrates. Pain relief reduces sympathetic stress response.

topic: Anticoagulation in ACS - Unfractionated Heparin and LMWH
content: Anticoagulation during ACS/PCI: unfractionated heparin (UFH) IV bolus 50-100 units/kg, then continuous infusion (goal aPTT 50-70 seconds). LMWH (enoxaparin) 1mg/kg IV bolus for PCI. UFH preferred if planned urgent angiography (reversible by protamine, shorter half-life). LMWH comparable efficacy, more predictable, used if conservative strategy. Target: prevent stent thrombosis, recurrent ACS. Duration: typically 24-48 hours for STEMI, shorter for stable NSTEMI. Check platelets for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT, rare but serious).

topic: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa Inhibitors - Use in PCI
content: GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban): potent antiplatelet agents, block final common pathway of platelet aggregation. Use in PCI (especially STEMI, thrombotic lesions): given IV bolus, then infusion. Abciximab 0.25mg/kg bolus, then 0.125 mcg/kg/min infusion. Reduces ischemic complications during PCI, improves outcomes. Cautions: bleeding risk (especially with dual antiplatelet therapy + anticoagulation), thrombocytopenia (check platelets), requires careful coordination with other antiplatelet agents. Used less frequently now (dual antiplatelet therapy + newer P2Y12 inhibitors effective).

topic: Calcium Channel Blockers in ACS - Limited Role
content: Calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil, nifedipine): generally avoided in acute STEMI/NSTEMI due to lack of mortality benefit vs beta-blockers. Verapamil/diltiazem non-dihydropyridines can worsen heart failure if EF reduced. Nifedipine (dihydropyridine) increases tachycardia/reflex activation, counterproductive. Limited role: rate control in NSTEMI if beta-blocker contraindicated/intolerant, or for hypertension control. No indication for routine use in ACS. Long-acting nifedipine acceptable for chronic CAD management post-MI.

topic: Aldosterone Antagonists in ACS with Reduced EF
content: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone): reduce mortality in post-MI heart failure with reduced EF (EF <40%). Typical: eplerenone 25mg daily, titrate to 50mg daily (or spironolactone 12.5-25mg daily). Mechanism: blocks aldosterone-mediated fibrosis, improves ventricular remodeling. Side effect: hyperkalemia risk (check baseline K+, renal function; recheck at 3-7 days, then periodically). Indication: documented reduced EF post-MI, not just during acute event. Continue indefinitely if tolerated.

topic: Cardiogenic Shock Post-MI - Pathophysiology and Management
content: Cardiogenic shock: hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) + evidence of hypoperfusion (altered mental status, cool extremities, oliguria, lactate >2) due to left ventricular dysfunction post-MI. Incidence 5-8% of acute MI, mortality 50-80%. Causes: extensive LV infarction (>40% LV mass), mechanical complications (MR, VSD, rupture), RV infarction, arrhythmias. Management: revascularization (emergency PCI, IABP, mechanical support), inotropes/vasopressors (dobutamine, milrinone, norepinephrine), diuretics (cautiously), monitor closely in ICU.

topic: Mechanical Complications - Mitral Regurgitation Post-MI
content: Acute mitral regurgitation post-MI: due to papillary muscle rupture (partial or complete) in posteromedial infarction (RCA territory 70%, LCx 20%). Presents with acute dyspnea, hypoxia, new holosystolic murmur, pulmonary edema. Diagnosis: echocardiography (color Doppler shows regurgitant jet). Partial rupture: medical management (vasodilators, inotropes) with urgent surgery. Complete rupture: cardiogenic shock, requires emergency mitral valve repair/replacement. Mortality high (mortality 50-70% if unrepaired).

topic: Mechanical Complications - Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) Post-MI
content: VSD post-MI: ventricular septal rupture within days of MI (usually anterior MI with LAD occlusion). Presents with new holosystolic murmur, abrupt hypotension, pulmonary edema, right-to-left shunt (hypoxia). Diagnosis: echocardiography with color Doppler (shunt flow visible), cardiac catheterization (O2 saturation step-up from RV to PA). Hemodynamically significant VSD requires urgent surgical repair (mortality 25-40% if surgery, >90% if medical management alone). IABP, vasodilators, inotropes temporary bridge to surgery.

topic: Mechanical Complications - Free Wall Rupture
content: Left ventricular free wall rupture: catastrophic complication (1-3% of MIs), usually 3-7 days post-MI, mortality >90%. Risk factors: first MI, anterior location, older age, female, delayed reperfusion, excessive anticoagulation. Presentation: sudden severe chest pain, hemodynamic collapse, tamponade physiology, pulseless electrical activity. Diagnosis: echo with pericardial fluid/hemopericardium, or clinical presentation. Management: emergency pericardiocentesis (temporary), then emergency surgery (repair patch, support). Subacute presentation (pseudoaneurysm) may allow delayed surgery.

topic: Post-Infarction Arrhythmias - Bradycardia and Conduction Blocks
content: Bradycardia/heart block post-MI: caused by ischemia of conducting tissue. Inferior MI (RCA): sinus bradycardia, AV blocks (Mobitz I/II, complete), usually transient. Anterior MI (LAD): His bundle ischemia, Mobitz II/complete block with wide QRS escape, poor prognosis. Management: atropine 0.5-1mg IV for symptomatic bradycardia (inferior MI responsive), temporary pacing if hemodynamic compromise, permanent pacing if persistent high-degree block (anterior MI). Avoid beta-blockers if bradycardia. Monitor telemetry closely.

topic: Post-Infarction Arrhythmias - Ventricular Fibrillation and Tachycardia
content: Ventricular fibrillation (VF): primary (within 48 hours of MI onset) or secondary (due to cardiogenic shock, pump failure). Primary VF: immediate defibrillation, ACLS protocol. Mortality 3-5% if treated promptly, >90% if delayed. Ventricular tachycardia (VT): can be sustained or non-sustained. Treat if hemodynamically unstable: immediate defibrillation if pulseless, amiodarone IV if hemodynamic tolerance. Beta-blockers reduce VT/VF risk. Long-term: ICD placement if EF <35 post-MI (ischemic cardiomyopathy).

topic: Left Ventricular Remodeling and Heart Failure Post-MI
content: Post-MI LV remodeling: acute dilation (within hours), then eccentric hypertrophy (days to weeks) if large MI. Results in reduced EF, heart failure symptoms. Prevention/slowing: early reperfusion (limits infarct size), beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, aldosterone antagonists, cardiac rehabilitation. LV thrombus risk: increased if anterior MI, large infarct, low EF, akinetic/dyskinetic segment. Prophylaxis: warfarin or DOAC if thrombus documented (goal INR 2-3), or if EF <30 + anterior MI + anterior akinesis (controversial). Echocardiography at discharge to assess EF, complications.

topic: Pericarditis and Dressler's Syndrome Post-MI
content: Post-MI pericarditis: inflammation from transmural infarction/pericardial irritation. Early (within 24-72 hours): pleuritic chest pain, pericardial rub, may mimic recurrent ischemia. Late (Dressler's syndrome, weeks-months post-MI): fever, pleurisy, pericarditis, pericardial effusion, sometimes with tamponade. Management: NSAIDs (aspirin, indomethacin), colchicine. Avoid in presence of reduced EF or fluid restriction needed. Steroids reserved for refractory cases. Distinguish from recurrent ischemia/infarction (troponin elevation more marked in infarction).

topic: Right Ventricular Infarction - Complications and Long-term Sequelae
content: RV infarction complications: hypotension (loss of RV contractility), bradycardia/AV blocks (nodal ischemia), atrial fibrillation (RA ischemia). Recurrent ischemia: RV infarction patients high risk; reperfusion critical. Long-term: most recover within days to weeks; persistent RV dysfunction rare. Tricuspid regurgitation may develop (secondary to RV dilatation). RV function assessed by echo; improvement typically occurs. Low mortality if uncomplicated by LV involvement or hemodynamic decompensation.

topic: Myocardial Rupture Variants - Papillary Muscle vs Septum vs Wall
content: Myocardial rupture mechanisms differ by location: (1) Papillary muscle: MR symptom, preserved systolic function initially; (2) Ventricular septum: VSD physiology, step-up in saturation; (3) Free wall: tamponade, shock, pulseless arrest. All occur 3-7 days post-MI typically. Risk: older age, first MI, female, lack of collaterals, hypertension in acute phase, excess anticoagulation. Prevention: early reperfusion, avoid excessive anticoagulation, control BP. Prognosis: free wall worst, VSD intermediate, MR variable depending on extent.

topic: Recurrent Angina Post-MI - Postinfarction Angina vs Reinfarction
content: Post-infarction angina: ischemia in different coronary territory from initial MI (not same vessel). Risk: incomplete revascularization, progression of CAD, stent restenosis. Presents with chest pain similar to initial MI. Troponin may be elevated from original MI (doesn't reset for 7-14 days). Serial troponins/ECG changes help distinguish (new elevation = reinfarction). Management: urgent catheterization/PCI if recurrent angina. Preventive: optimal medical therapy (dual antiplatelet, beta-blockers, ACE-I, statins, revascularization), smoking cessation, risk factor control.

topic: Post-MI Discharge Planning and Medication Optimization
content: Discharge medications (essential): dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor), beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, high-intensity statin, consider aldosterone antagonist if EF <40%. Dosing optimization: beta-blocker target HR 50-60, SBP 100-120; ACE-I titrate to maximum tolerated. Discharge checklist: smoking cessation counseling, cardiac rehabilitation referral, follow-up cardiology appointment, PCI documentation, EF assessment (echo), ICD consideration if EF <35 post-stabilization (30 days post-MI).

topic: Cardiac Rehabilitation Post-MI
content: Cardiac rehabilitation: supervised exercise training, education on risk factor modification, psychosocial support. Benefits: improved functional capacity, reduced mortality (20-30% RRR), improved quality of life. Phases: Phase I (acute hospitalization), Phase II (3-6 weeks post-discharge, supervised supervised outpatient), Phase III (long-term home-based). Components: aerobic exercise (target 150 min/week moderate intensity), dietary counseling (heart-healthy diet, DASH), smoking cessation, stress management, medication education. Refer all post-MI patients; contraindications rare (hemodynamic instability, ongoing ischemia).

topic: Risk Factor Modification - Smoking, Lipids, Blood Pressure
content: Post-MI secondary prevention: (1) Smoking cessation: counseling + pharmacotherapy (varenicline, bupropion) reduces cardiac events 50%+. (2) Lipid targets: LDL <70, or <55 if very high risk; use high-intensity statins, consider ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitors if LDL not at goal. (3) Blood pressure: target <130/80 (higher targets if dialysis/advanced CKD). (4) Diabetes: tight glucose control (target HbA1c 7% non-fragile), GLP-1 agonist/SGLT2i for cardioprotection. (5) Physical activity: 150 min/week moderate intensity, resistance training 2x/week.

topic: Anticoagulation Strategy Post-PCI - DAPT vs Anticoagulation
content: Anticoagulation post-PCI: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) standard. Additional anticoagulation (UFH/LMWH/fondaparinux) during acute phase only (typically 24-48 hours). Long-term oral anticoagulation (warfarin/DOAC) indicated if: (1) LV thrombus, (2) atrial fibrillation, (3) hypercoagulable state. Balance between thrombotic (stent thrombosis, recurrent MI) and bleeding risks. Triple therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 + anticoagulation) increases bleeding risk significantly; requires careful patient selection. Proton pump inhibitor for GI bleed prophylaxis if triple therapy.

topic: ICD and CRT Indications Post-MI
content: ICD indication: reduced EF ≤35% at >40 days post-MI (allow time for recovery). Placement: single-chamber ICD if sinus rhythm no indication for pacing, dual-chamber if bradycardia/need for rate-responsive pacing, biventricular ICD if QRS >120ms + symptomatic heart failure (CRT-D). Wearable defibrillator temporary option if EF 25-35% and uncertain recovery. Prevents sudden cardiac death, improves survival in ischemic cardiomyopathy. Refer to EP for evaluation if EF <35% at 6 weeks.

topic: Ischemia Testing and Viability Assessment Post-MI
content: Stress testing (exercise treadmill, stress echo, nuclear) at 3-6 weeks post-MI to assess for inducible ischemia (risk stratification). Indications: intermediate EF, symptoms suggesting ongoing ischemia, equivocal revascularization. Viability testing (stress echo, nuclear imaging, late-gadolinium enhancement MRI) identifies potentially salvageable myocardium (>50% wall thickness) in akinetic/dyskinetic segments. Viability presence suggests consideration for revascularization in heart failure (ISCHEMIA-CHF, STICH trials showed modest benefit). Absence of viability: medical management. Coronary angiography already performed during acute PCI usually; additional testing guides management.

topic: Depression Screening and Mental Health Post-MI
content: Post-MI depression: 20-30% incidence, associated with poor outcomes, reduced adherence, increased mortality. Screening: PHQ-9 or Depression Anxiety Stress Scale. Intervention: cognitive-behavioral therapy, exercise (proven effective), SSRIs if moderate-severe (sertraline, citalopram; avoid tricyclics). Anxiety common; treated similarly. Participation in cardiac rehab provides psychosocial support. Psychological distress predicts adverse outcomes; addressing mental health integral to secondary prevention.

topic: Long-term Follow-up and Medication Adherence
content: Post-MI long-term follow-up: cardiology visits at 1-2 weeks, 4-6 weeks, then 3-6 months, then annually. Assess: medication adherence, side effects, symptoms of heart failure/angina, functional status, risk factor control. Medication adherence critical: dual antiplatelet therapy adherence 50% at 12 months without intervention. Interventions: simplify regimen (once-daily dosing), patient education, reminder systems, medication reconciliation. Non-adherence is major cause of stent thrombosis, recurrent events, poor outcomes. Regular follow-up improves adherence and identifies problems early.
